body_markdown:
Over 70 classic cars crossed the block on October 10 during[the Aguttes Autoworld 2026](https://www.aguttes.com/catalogue/autoworld-2026-auction-motion-9e101f07-fb8f-455c-8e0d-1473283f402c?limit=96) sale held in Brussels, Belgium. The catalog included the usual suspects, such as a 1977 Porsche 911 Targa and a 21-window 1965 Volkswagen Bus, as well as newer models that recently made the transition from the local classifieds to the international auction circuit, as well as a few compelling oddballs. The results shed light on what the meat of the collector-car market looks like on the other side of the pond. Here are five highlights that caught our eye.


## 1952 Mercedes-Benz 170D Pickup


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


[Lot 69](https://www.aguttes.com/lot/autoworld-2026-auction-motion-9e101f07-fb8f-455c-8e0d-1473283f402c/1952-mercedes-benz-170-d-879a3e11-0a3c-4473-8339-beeb840441ed)


Released in 1935, the Mercedes-Benz W136 was available in a dizzying number of configurations. Buyers could order a sedan, a limousine, and a cabriolet—all body styles normally associated with the German brand—but a pickup was offered in some markets. Juan Manuel Fangio reportedly commissioned the pickup variant in order to sell it through his dealership in Argentina.


Finding a pickup today is easier said than done; few were built and not many survived, but the Aguttes catalog included a 1952 170D that sold for €29,840 (about $33,400). It’s powered by a four-cylinder diesel engine, and it was restored a few years ago.


## 1981 BMW 735i


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


[Lot 45](https://www.aguttes.com/lot/autoworld-2026-auction-motion-9e101f07-fb8f-455c-8e0d-1473283f402c/1981-bmw-735i-a6102e18-56c2-4090-a755-b0950be24da3)


If you’re looking for proof that you don’t need a CEO’s budget to win a cool car at an auction, this is it. It’s a 1981 BMW 735i with a five-speed stick, a blue cloth interior, and a 1986-issue Parisian registration number that hints at long-term ownership. It looks like a relatively clean, unmodified car, though the auction description notes that the power steering system needs to be serviced and that the fuel gauge isn’t accurate. It sold for €10,742 (about $12,000), which is right in the middle of its pre-auction estimate.


That’s a lot of car for the money, and a reasonable amount of money for a cool, unique car. BMW’s classic 5 Series and 7 Series are often overlooked by collectors in favor of the nimbler 3 Series, yet they make an excellent entry point into classic-car ownership.


## 1984 Sbarro Super Eight


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes


[Lot 42](https://www.aguttes.com/lot/autoworld-2026-auction-motion-9e101f07-fb8f-455c-8e0d-1473283f402c/1980-sbarro-super-eight-dc65e493-4a12-4bfe-92d2-02df9e91eb06)


Undoubtedly one of the most unique cars in the Aguttes Autoworld 2026 sale, this 1984 Sbarro Super Eight is a one-off positioned at the unlikely intersection of city cars and supercars. It stretches 118 inches long, so it’s about the same size as the original Mini, yet it’s powered by a Ferrari 308 GTB-sourced, 3.0-liter V-8 rated at roughly 240 horsepower. The engine is linked to a gated five-speed manual transmission that also comes from the 308 GTB. The entire body is made out of fiberglass to keep weight in check.


Aguttes explains that the Super Eight was developed with the help of a Swiss industrialist named Bernd Grohe, who was also its original owner. It has spent most of its life in private collections, but it sounds like it’s been maintained and driven on at least a semi-regular basis. Its odometer displays roughly 30,000 kilometers (about 19,000 miles) and the belts were changed in 2020.


Registered in Holland but not currently inspected, this head-turning one-off sold for €105,036 (about $117,400). It fell well short of the pre-auction estimate that was pegged at between €120,000 and €180,000 (around $134,000 and $201,100, respectively).


## 1989 Renault Super 5 GT Turbo


Aguttes


Aguttes


Aguttes

[Lot 41](https://www.aguttes.com/lot/autoworld-2026-auction-motion-9e101f07-fb8f-455c-8e0d-1473283f402c/1989-renault-supercinq-gt-turbo-0659dc0c-28fa-409e-90b9-9251703792d6)


Largely stock and finished in a relatively subtle shade of black, this Renault Super 5 GT Turbo confirms that 1980s performance icons are still in hot demand. It sold for €31,033 (about $34,800), which is near the top end of the pre-auction estimate provided by Aguttes. Tellingly, a 1970 Alfa Romeo GT 1300 Junior Zagato[sold for just a few thousand euros more](https://www.aguttes.com/lot/autoworld-2026-auction-motion-9e101f07-fb8f-455c-8e0d-1473283f402c/1970-alfa-romeo-gt-1300-junior-zagato-97af2e5e-4a8a-4df4-9e14-de4570ee31f6) at the Aguttes Autoworld 2026 sale. The two cars were built nearly 20 years apart, which illustrates[a trend we’ve written about before](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-collector-car-market-is-seeing-an-influx-of-younger-cars/) : Younger buyers are entering the market; they want the cars that they lusted after as kids, and they’re willing to pay a premium for the right example.


Sold on a Belgian title, this 1989 model is a desirable second-series car with more modern styling than first-series examples and a 1.4-liter four-cylinder engine turbocharged to 120 horsepower. While that might not sound like much, keep in mind that the Super 5 GT Turbo tips the scale at about 1,820 pounds. It’s lighter and quicker than a 16-valve Volkswagen Golf GTI from the same era.


## 1998 BMW M3

[Lot 40](https://www.aguttes.com/lot/autoworld-2026-auction-motion-9e101f07-fb8f-455c-8e0d-1473283f402c/1998-bmw-m3-e36-c347b054-17f7-4402-9d62-e78cf1091b50)


Finding another[E36-generation BMW M3](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/market-spotlight/your-handy-1995-99-bmw-e36-m3-buyers-guide/) that ticks the same boxes as this example will be easier said than done. It’s a European-market car with the 321-horsepower straight-six, its odometer shows a little over 34,000 miles, and it’s finished in Dakar Yellow.


Aguttes notes that this car’s history is particularly well documented, which is another big selling point. It was sold new in Italy, and it remained with its original owner until it was sold to a collector in the Czech Republic in 2008. The second owner was particularly fond of low-mileage cars, so it’s safe to assume that this M3 wasn’t driven much during his ownership. The seller, who also collects low-mileage cars, has owned this M3 since 2018. It’s reportedly entirely original, including the paint and the interior.


The cool factor explains the selling price: €67,067 (about $69,500). That’s near the top end of the E36 M3 market, excluding GT cars, Lightweight models, and celebrity-owned examples. Well bought, or well sold? Share your thoughts in the comments below.
